claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain and toughness relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
The plastic strain and toughness of WTaTiVZr are governed by nanoscale lattice distortions from its multielement solid solution.
These lattice distortions lower the effective Peierls barrier for dislocation motion.
These lattice distortions promote crack-tip blunting.
Lowering the Peierls barrier and promoting crack-tip blunting enable more distributed plastic deformation and delay brittle fracture.
The proposed WTaTiVZr test material is equimolar and has a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
A comparison with pure tungsten tested under identical processing, temperature, and environmental conditions is proposed as the control.
Temperatures of approximately 1200–1600°C are representative of high-temperature plasma-facing-component service.
Inert-atmosphere testing can limit extrinsic oxidation effects during the comparison.
Atomic size and modulus mismatch among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces nanoscale lattice distortions.
The lattice distortions may promote subtle local compositional fluctuations without gross second-phase formation.
Ta, Ti, V, and Zr are refractory, low-activation alloying elements in the proposed system.
Local lattice strains reduce the barriers to dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Local lattice strains create effective crack-tip shielding.
The proposed mechanism reduces dislocation pile-up and brittle cleavage.
Pure tungsten has a higher Peierls barrier and fewer mechanisms for stress redistribution than equimolar WTaTiVZr.
WTaTiVZr will have higher elongation to failure and plastic strain than pure tungsten at 1200–1600°C.
WTaTiVZr will have greater fracture toughness and energy absorption before crack propagation than pure tungsten at 1200–1600°C.
WTaTiVZr will have lower yield stress than pure tungsten under the specified high-temperature conditions.
The mechanism is expected to apply only while microstructural homogeneity is maintained and may fail under substantial phase segregation, oxidation, or irradiation-induced damage.
